utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-65-PT, the Prosecutor versus Zeljko Meakic, Momcilo Gruban, Dusan Fustar, Predrag Banovic and Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Sureta Chana appearing for the Prosecution. I'm assisted by Katharina Margetts and David Leese is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Counsel Slobodanka Nedic from Belgrade with my learned co-counsel Thomas Moran representing Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This being the oral hearing on a Defence motion for provisional release filed on behalf of this accused, the parties can take it that we have read the motion and the response. Accordingly there is no need for repetition of those. But we will hear any submissions that anybody wishes to make. Ms. Nedic, I think it's for you to begin on behalf of the applicant, the motion. Just one moment. Judge Kwon kindly reminds me that we have here the representative of the Republika Srpska; is that right? Perhaps he would like to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, my name is Trivun Jovicic, I am minister, counsel and liaison officer of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nedic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence team of Dusko Knezevic my colleague Thomas Moran will address you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first we have some documents which are copies of official documents. They have been provided to the Prosecution and we would move to introduce those. They are Mr. Knezevic's marriage certificate, his birth certificate, and a statement from the police that he is not a criminal -- that he has no criminal record and finally we have a copy of a wanted poster produced by the Tribunal and it's the only copy we have. It's a bad copy, and it was provided for us, I believe, by the OTP. We do not have the original, have never had access to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour we were just provided these documents about three minutes ago. We do object to Defence counsel admitting them into evidence at this stage. We do not have such a problem with the marriage certificate and the birth certificate, Your Honour, but in respect of this what Defence counsel calls his criminal record, Your Honour, the Prosecution would have liked to have sometime to investigate this. The Defence counsel had ample time, Your Honour, to produce this document. It is their motion and they had filed their response sometime ago and they produce it as of now. We would like an adjournment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal first of all with the matters which are not subject to dispute. The marriage certificate, if you produce that, the birth certificate, and presumably there is no dispute as far as the wanted poster is concerned. Mr. Moran you've heard what the Prosecution say about the record. Is there any reason why it wasn't produced before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think Ms. Nedic may have more information as to that. I don't know how long we've had it. I have not had it before yesterday. But Ms. Nedic may have had it a little before then. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, how long do you want to investigate this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at the document I've just had an opportunity to do so, it's about three lines and it says that it's not registered in criminal evidence at this station. It gives no date, it gives no duration for his not registered. It's absolutely got no particulars whatsoever. I suggest Your Honours, that it's -- that the document in itself, because it lacks the particulars, should not be admitted into evidence at all, otherwise it would be a waste of the Court's time to grant an adjournment for us to investigate this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we'll do is we will enter it, we will mark it for identification, we will give the Prosecution two weeks from today to investigate it, and to make any submissions about it. So we won't render our decision on this matter until they've had an opportunity which they should have, obviously, to investigate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, also since it's a document under seal we have a representative from Republika Srpska who is qualified to testify this is the seal of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever. We will give them time to investigate it but we will introduce it for the purposes of marking it for identification. Yes. We'll continue with the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour. Okay. Your Honour at this time we would like to call Mr. Knezevic as a witness for the purposes of this hearing only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, time is limited but we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it shouldn't take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will, Mr. Moran, we were asking ourselves whether this had ever been done before, certainly not before our Trial Chamber has an accused given evidence at this stage but provided it's limited to about ten minutes, we can see no reason why he shouldn't give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour if I may, in respect of this, the Prosecution would object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You would object? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, if Mr. Knezevic is going to give evidence we should have a statement upon which we can test his veracity and investigate it and prepare our cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't we see what he says, and see whether there is any need for you to have an adjournment to examine what he says. This is only an interlocutory hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, we stand guided by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Nedic will question Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you want him to testify from there or would you like him go witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He better go into the witness box, the usual way. Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, would you like to take a seat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Nedic you will of course be limiting your examination to matters relevant purely to this hearing on provisional release nothing more than that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness give us his full name for the record and his date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusko Knezevic, I was born on the 17th of June, 1967, in Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, sit down by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a bit more about where you were born, where you attended school and what did you do upon completion of your schooling?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary school in Prijedor, as well as my secondary school for catering.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I am. I have a wife and a five year old son who was born in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Where was your son born and where were you married and when?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: My son was born in Prijedor on the 1st of December, 1997, whereas I got married in 1993. My official wedding date was the 14th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, I would like to ask you this: After the birth of your son, did you continue living in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Prijedor until the 11th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Where did you live following that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Since there was no work for me, in Prijedor, I used to sell fruits and vegetables at the marketplace in Prijedor, and since that wasn't sufficient, as a source of income, my wife and I decided to go to Belgrade and to see whether we could have a better existence there. I went to Belgrade on the 11th of April, 1998. I started looking for work there. The situation in Serbia was quite difficult as well. I was unable to find work in my own profession, and I started working at the flea market in Belgrade in Pancevo, I was selling clothing and that provided a modest source of income for me. In the beginning of 2002, I saw my photograph among other accused. That was in 2002. I was shocked to see my photograph. I couldn't believe that it was me. As I didn't know what to do, what to do with my family and where to look for assistance, I turned to my friend. I called him in Prijedor and that was Miodrag Deretic an attorney there. I called him on the telephone, telling him I would like to talk to him about something. Mr. Deretic told me that he was busy with his own work and that I should call him in several days. He said that he might come to Belgrade about some business of his. So after several days, I called him again, and we agreed to meet in downtown Belgrade. We met in Belgrade, we went to have a drink, we talked about every day problems, and finally I told him that I called him for one reason. I told him that I had seen my photograph on the wanted poster of The Hague Tribunal. Mr. Deretic replied to me that he was aware of that and that my indictment was not of a light nature, and that if proven, I could be sentenced to a long sentence. I told Mr. Deretic, regardless of any possible sentence or any charges, I've decided to surrender. Mr. Deretic told me that I should think about it carefully first, to see whether it was a good idea and that I shouldn't make a decision too quickly, to which I responded that I have firmly decided to surrender to The Hague Tribunal and to come before it regardless of the nature of the charges. I will go to The Hague and try to defend myself. Therefore, I asked Mr. Deretic to represent me before The Hague Tribunal to arrange with the Tribunal and the authorities of Republika Srpska my voluntary surrender. He told me he was unable to do that immediately and that he needed sometime for that. We agreed that I should call him on the telephone again in Prijedor. I did that. And I asked him whether there was anything new, how were things going? And he told me, call me back in two or three days, I will know how things are. I did that. I called him in two or three days, and he said that my surrender had been scheduled for the 18th of May, 2002. I wish to point out that nobody exerted any pressure to make me surrender. That was purely my own decision, my own and nobody else's. Following everything that was done by Mr. Deretic with the Tribunal, and authorities of Republika Srpska, I told him to also inform my family of my decision. I think that I did not make a mistake in coming here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, I would like you to go back to the early 2002. Tell us, please, where did you see your photograph on the wanted poster? How did you learn that you were on the wanted poster?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I happened to see my picture by chance on television. I was sitting watching television and then there were photographs of The Hague indictees shown, and there I saw my photograph. That was in early 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, while you lived in Serbia, in Belgrade, did you live there under your own name? Did you have documents issued in your own name then? Where did you live at the time? Did your neighbours know you under your real name or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in Belgrade, in Divcibarska Street number 8, I used my own last name and all the neighbours knew me there as Dusko Knezevic as well as my wife and my son. I never had any false documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Should the Trial Chamber decide to grant your request for provisional release, do you have a plan as to where you're going to live and what are you going to do for a living if the provisional release request is granted?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would like to live with my family, to work, to find an employment, to provide subsistence for my family, and should The Hague Tribunal call me at any time of day or night, I am prepared to come here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Are you also prepared to abide by any rulings or requests, should there be such, if the Court grants your request?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm ready to abide by any kind of rulings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: And that means what?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That means that I will come any time the Tribunal calls me to come here, regardless of the time of the day, I will come here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Are you prepared to abide by Tribunal's ruling to report regularly to police authorities?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Any kind of request contained in the Tribunal's ruling, I will abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is a guarantee for your employment should you be granted provisional release, as well as a guarantee for your temporary housing until you're able to find permanent housing for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: You have a written guarantee for employment in Bijeljina and temporary housing in the Drina hotel should you find regular housing, are you prepared to inform both the Tribunal and the authorities in Republika Srpska about your permanent place of residence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: As far as the witnesses are concerned, are you prepared to give a promise here before this Chamber that you will refrain from establishing any kind of contact with witnesses and that you will not try to intimidate the witness?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I will not establish any contact with witnesses, nor will I attempt to intimidate them, as I was able to see from the material provided to me, I don't know these witnesses, nor do I know where they live or what they do for a living.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following: Before the indictment was issued against you by The Hague Tribunal, were you ever convicted for a crime prior to that? Were there any proceedings instigated against you? Were there any charges against you for any crime?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never ever convicted of any crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, we have been considering the position and the fact that you have had no notice of this intention to cross-examine. We think if at all possible, you should deal with the matter today because we don't want to waste any further time on it but what we will do, since you've got two weeks to consider the other matter, if there are any matters which you come across during that time, which you wish to put before us, which contradict what the accused has said in his evidence, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then you'll have leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge May, just one thing for the record. We discussed it and we are going to withdraw the exhibit they objected to. They can still have their two weeks but we are going to withdraw that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. They can still have their two weeks it having been put in and they can also have two weeks to find anything which they wish to put before the Tribunal if they can to contradict the evidence the witness has given. But if you want to ask any questions now about -- purely about that evidence, you can, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic you said you lived in Prijedor most of your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of my life. I've been in Prijedor since 1986. In 1987 I went to the army. I got a job, I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said you went to catering school. Which catering school was this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The catering school that trains waiters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Does it have a name?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does have a name but I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How long were you at this catering school, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what year was this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was it ten years ago, five years ago, any idea?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly how many years that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, do you know a man called Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's outside the scope of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Let's see what the purpose of the question is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Zigic, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I know him from the class band. He played in a band called class. That is the only way that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And are you aware that in 1995, you were first indicted with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, again, Your Honour this is outside the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may affect it because one of the lines which -- one of the points he's making is that he first became aware of this -- these matters when he saw this poster. So if Zigic was indicted in 1995 it may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you aware, then, Mr. Knezevic, that you were indicted with Zoran Zigic in 1995, which was the first time this poster --

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you see this poster that your Defence counsel has submitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I saw the poster on television, in early 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I think you stated earlier on in your evidence, Your Honour, we can have a look at it, that in 2000, you realised that this -- you did see the poster but it was the wrong birth date. That is also what has been alleged by your counsel in his written motion.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that it's a mistake but I know what I saw in 2002, in early 2002 and I saw it personally on television where I was flabbergasted to see my photograph on television and to see the wanted poster. I couldn't believe my eyes at what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But you were aware that Zoran Zigic was indicted in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: How could I know that Mr. Zigic was indicted in 1995 when I never socialised with Mr. Zoran Zigic? I didn't have any contacts with him. First of all I have my own family. I'm taking care of my family. Not about any individuals in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is it your position then Mr. Knezevic that in March, 1996, this poster, that your counsel has submitted into evidence, is a photograph of Zoran Zigic and yourself in the same poster?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, I never saw any photographs until 2002, never. I simply didn't. I wasn't interested in that, and why would I see anything like that? And even this one that I saw, I only happened to see that by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you said you -- the reason that you surrendered is in 2002 is because you saw the poster and you were shocked, to put it in your words?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I was absolutely out of my mind when I saw that. I was very surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is it not also true, Mr. Knezevic, that you surrendered because in 2002, the Belgrade authorities were beginning to cooperate with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You're aware that a warrant of arrest had been issued for you as far back as 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: If you know, that's okay, but I don't know, and I said when I first became aware of it, and that was in early 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And there was another correct version of that -- of the warrant in 1999. Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware that Zigic, Zoran Zigic, transferred around 1998 to the seat of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely did not follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a trial, proceeding, for in respect of the Omarska camp where Zoran Zigic was one of the accused and it was on TV and got much publicity in the media?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that either. I didn't have time to follow television or to read newspapers. I had to make a living for myself and my family. So I wasn't interested in some things.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What were you doing while you were making this living? Where were you working all this time where you do not have time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I said that first of all I worked in Prijedor at the green market selling fruit and vegetables and in 1998, I went to Serbia and I worked at the flea market in Belgrade and the flea market in Pancevo from early morning until evening. I didn't have time even to rest properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So it means that were you not employed anywhere in all this time? You were just at flea markets? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I worked. I bought goods and sold them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were not employed? You were self-employed?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't my own. I don't know if I need to explain to you how it works.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you employed or were you self-employed? It's quite simple, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I worked for myself. I was self-employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, can I just ask to you clarify something? Did you put to the accused that in his motion, it is said that he first saw the poster in 2000? Did you put that to him, that that is in his motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's in the written motion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is so, then perhaps you could have your assistant try to find the page and at the end of your cross-examination, you can bring that to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, just to --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic to go back when you said that you had absolutely no idea that you -- that your name had appeared in any poster, in -- while were you in Prijedor because you were busy in your flea markets, is it true that no one in Prijedor told you that your name is on this poster and that in fact you're wanted by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me, absolutely nobody. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr. Knezevic, that nobody told you that your friend Zoran Zigic and you had been accused of being together while you committed these crimes at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that, that, one, goes well beyond the scope of this hearing, and two, this hearing is not on the merits of guilt or innocence. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is not of guilt or innocence but whether he heard anybody told him that he was accused, simply accused, of being with Zigic committing crimes. That's the question. It doesn't go to guilt or innocence. Yes, Mr. Knezevic, what's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am replying that no one told me, I didn't know that Zoran Zigic was on the wanted list of The Hague Tribunal. I was taking care of my family, and I wasn't bothering about Zoran Zigic or any other person.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you said you have a wife, Mr. Knezevic. Did she never come and tell you that people in the Prijedor region are talking about a wanted poster with your face on it with Zoran Zigic, your friend?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your counsel has asked you a question to which you responded in the positive, that you have an offer of employment by a Mr. -- one Lanko [phoen]. Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There is an offer of employment in Bijeljina, do you know who this offer of employment is by?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Do I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You don't know that you have -- you don't know that you have an offer of employment in Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: To get a job, to work, yes, that is my wish, to start to work so that I can support my family. I don't want to end up on the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is whether you know who it is who has offered you employment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Slajian [phoen] Lanko.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: He's in the catering business.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Mr. Knezevic. What is his relationship to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The man would like to make it possible for me to work so that my family and I could live and we could -- I could make a living by working on his premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Knezevic? Why is he offering you this employment?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he's offering it to me. I am not supposed to end up on the street, am I?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I know what -- that he is offering it to you but do you have any connection? How long have you known him and why is he offering you this employment?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why I would need to have a connection in order to be offered a job. I have a desire to work. I am prepared to work, and after all, my family needs funds in order to live. It's better for me to work honestly than to steal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So can I take it from that that you really do not know Mr. Lanko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've probably taken this as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It would be just one last one on the point of --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When the Omarska trial was taking place, Mr. Knezevic, it was broadcasted on TV in Bosnia. Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I've already said that I didn't watch television or read the newspapers. I really didn't have time. I had a lot of work to do in Prijedor and in Belgrade as well, from morning to night.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you are aware, Mr. Knezevic, that the witnesses who testified in this trial actually took your name as one of the people who were at the camps beating up the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he says he's heard nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So nobody ever told you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that will be all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, unless you have any further questions, thank you Mr. Knezevic, if you'd like to go back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have about half an hour left before we have to adjourn this matter. Quarter of an hour each if you want it. As I say we've already read the motion so there is no need to repeat what's been said. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I believe the representative of the Republika Srpska if the Court wants to hear it will personally tell the Court that Republika Srpska will guarantee his appearance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to do that before you address us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour if he wants to take a few minutes and give the personal guarantee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovicic is there anything you would like to say? You've come here. I expect that Mr. Moran would wish you to -- and Ms. Nedic would wish to you repeat at least orally what it is you put in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for making it possible for me to reiterate the guarantees of Republika Srpska, which it has provided in this case. As you already know in several earlier cases, where the Trial Chamber has granted the provisional release, the government of Republika Srpska has wholly respected its obligations, which it has undertaken before the Tribunal. There wasn't one single remark made about the way the guarantees were implemented. All persons who have been provisionally released so far have wholly adhered to the rulings by the Trial Chambers. As well as the government of Republika Srpska, where these persons were returned at the request of the court, at the time and place requested by the Court. I think that there is no need to repeat that the government is willing to provide additional guarantees if so required. Also, I would like to emphasise that this is the first case of voluntary surrender with the cooperation of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, were you able to find the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Your Honour, it would appear that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Your Honour, it would appear that on page 3, where he says, well, the original indictments were -- years before Knezevic surrendered to the Tribunal. He did not know he was of indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, no, it was in the spring of 2002, Your Honour, it would appear I was mistaken. It was in the spring of 2002 that the Tribunal's corrected wanted poster appeared and there after he surrendered so Your Honour it would appear that I had not -- it was not exactly 2002 -- 2000. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I thought, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just quick arguments, Rule 65(B) sets a pretty straightforward legal standard. We have to convince you, present evidence to you that's believable that to prove to a preponderance that our client will appear when you tell him to be here, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that while he's released, he will not pose a danger to himself or others. This Trial Chamber and other Trial Chambers have pretty well held that voluntary surrender is very good evidence of a person's willingness to appear. I think Mr. Knezevic may be the only person only defendant in this Tribunal or at least the only one that I know of who has been congratulated by the official spokesman for the United States government for voluntary surrender. He'll execute any kind of bond, any kind of promise to appear that this Trial Chamber sets out. We have the guarantee of the Republika Srpska. We have his testimony that he's never been convicted of a crime. He's been promised a job and a place to live. Ms. Nedic went out and found him a place to live and found him a job so that we could present to this Tribunal a release plan to show that we just didn't want to leave him out on the streets. He's not some kind of a top level official. He's not some kind of person that a state is likely to protect. And the residents that we are asking the Tribunal to order is some distance from Prijedor and there is a reason for that, Your Honours. The reason for that is to help show a guarantee of protection of victims, witnesses and other persons. We don't know where any of these witnesses live. None -- nobody on the Defence side does. But it's pretty unlikely that they would be living in some little village 300 kilometres away from Prijedor. You can set conditions for provisional release to guarantee both the public safety and his appearance and I've just come up with a few that I've seen here or in other courts, regularly visiting the police station, you can have him sign in at the local police station on his way to work, on his way home. You can restrict him to a specific geographical area, if it's feasible, we would welcome electronic monitoring. To have him have an ankle bracelet on so that it shows where he is. If that's not feasible the Trial Chamber can set a curfew, require him to be at his home during non-working hours, and the Registry or the local police can randomly call him. If he doesn't answer the phone or if he's not called to the phone he's broken your curfew and you can deal with it then. Prosecutor argues that he's facing a substantial sentence. Well, so is everybody else in front of this Tribunal. The punishment for every offence in this Tribunal, the statutory punishment is the same, up to the rest of your life in the penitentiary. Prosecution has also laid out a few other arguments I believe are specious arguments, the first one is where they said that he doesn't undertake to tell you that he has no intention not to ask for -- no intention to ask for a change of residence. First thing, I'll tell you we don't have any intention of doing that. Second thing is, even if he did have an intention of doing that, this Trial Chamber would be in control of allowing him to have a change of residence. And the Prosecution's argument on that seems to presume that you won't do your job, that you'll just rubber stamp what we ask for and I don't believe that that's correct. They said we presented no evidence of an incorrect wanted poster and no signed undertakings or affidavits that's why we asked for an oral hearing, to present evidence. He got on that witness stand and he told you exactly what his undertaking would be. You tell him to be here, he'll be here. Again, just to close, on the protection of the witnesses and victims and other parties, Judge, my crystal ball is a little hazy, I can't tell the future very well and that's essentially what we are having -- what everybody has to do is predict whether or not -- not Mr. Knezevic but anybody else asking for provisional release what their actions will be in the future. I submit to you that his past actions, including voluntary surrender, show that he is unlikely to commit acts of violence or other acts against any of the victims or witnesses in this proceeding. He's told you he wouldn't, he doesn't know where they live, and secondly, we've asked him to be placed in an area some distance from the scene of the offences. And one of the reasons for that is to help protect witnesses. This Trial Chamber is quite capable of setting conditions of release that would meet both prongs of the Rule 65(B) standard and we ask you to release him on provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honour, the two preconditions of 65 have to be satisfied by the accused in this Court and they have to be satisfied to a burden of beyond -- to a balance of probabilities. That first he will not interfere with witnesses and he'll not pose any danger to victims and witnesses, sorry, and that he will appear for trial. Your Honours, the removal of exceptional circumstances does not make release -- there should not be a presumption of release in favour of the accused because exceptional circumstances is no longer in our rule. All factors which are usually taken into account when determining provisional release in national jurisdictions must still be taken into account, i.e. the gravity of the offences and the likely sentence, the crime -- it will attract if convicted. Your Honours, in national jurisdictions the Court seldom grants provisional release if the crimes are very grave and will attract a very onerous sentence upon conviction. Even if one was to adopt the same approach taken in national jurisdictions, it is inevitable that a Tribunal would grant provisional release less frequently than in other legal systems. Even if provisional release is granted slightly more often today than it was some years ago, Your Honour, it could never be suggested that it's easier to get provisional release from the Tribunal than it is in a national jurisdiction. The simple fact is that it is inconceivable that a national court would grant provisional release to a person charged with 31 counts of murder and 21 counts of personal violence. I suspect, Your Honours, that no court in a national jurisdiction has ever entertained such an application. I suspect that the accused is seeking to make legal history in doing so today. The burden of proof which is on the accused, Your Honours, is not a light one and the Tribunal's jurisprudence confirms that the accused has a substantial burden in persuading the Trial Chamber that he will appear for trial. And when it comes to the second of the preconditions in Rule 65(B) the jurisprudence of this Tribunal recognises an almost absolute burden on the accused to show an absence of danger to others. In the Blaskic case Your Honour the Trial Chamber found it could not be certain that if released the accused not pose a danger to any victims, witnesses or other person. In light of that fact that the knowledge which as an accused person he has of the evidence produced by the Prosecutor would place him in a situation permitting him to exert pressures on victims and witnesses and the investigation of the case would be seriously flawed. The Defence basically has produced two arguments, Your Honour, the voluntary surrender of the accused and the fact that there are guarantees from the Republika Srpska, and they also offered this employment that he's going to get in Bijeljina if he's to be provisionally released. We have just heard from counsel that the job was given to him and found for him by his counsel, and therefore he has no connection and in his cross-examination, he conceded the fact that he does not know this man at all. So I don't know what guarantee there is that the accused will continue in that employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, did he make that concession?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well he says he just knows him but he has no connection with him. He didn't say that but what he did say was when I asked him what is your connection. And he said, well he just wants to give me a job and counsel did say from the bar that the counsel said that he was not -- this was the job that the counsel found for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know how the 31 counts of murder break down under 7(1) and 7(3)?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have in our schedule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just remind me of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's schedule E, Your Honour, and schedule F, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. under schedule annex A and it's also in the pre-trial brief under annex A. Out of which, Your Honour, there are five murders which he personally committed and 13 beatings which he personally perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused has said that his voluntary surrender shows a willingness to cooperate with the International Tribunal as well as an indicator that he will appear for trial. And they offer that as the best proof that he will appear for trial as ordered by the Tribunal. We are as we have outlined in our motion, not entirely satisfied with the voluntary nature of the surrender and we suggest that the reason he surrendered at the time was because there was cooperation between the Republika Srpska and the Tribunal at that time, but he did remain at large, Your Honours, for seven years. He denies that he knows Zoran Zigic, and he denies that at no time in the Prijedor region that he was aware that he had been indicted by this Tribunal. The evidence, it is clear from the charge sheet, Your Honour, that he committed a lot of the crimes in the company of Zoran Zigic. So I feel that he's just taking the most pragmatic approach to his predicament and he's telling less than the truth. And the fact that he did voluntary surrender cannot in itself, Your Honours, be taken to satisfy this Court that the accused will appear for trial or interfere with witnesses. It would undermine the public confidence, not to say anything about the victims and the witnesses if he's released into the community only 270 kilometres from the crimes where they were committed and now we've heard that his connection to Bijeljina is very tenuous, and there is no reason to think that he will stay there or he will continue with his employment there. The counsel suggests he's a man with a stable background and he has good work record and yet the accused has just come before Your Honours and said to you that he has no -- he has never been employed in the past.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, no proof whatsoever has been provided to this Chamber as to where -- what the accused has been doing in all this time. He has now come before us on evidence given not under oath, Your Honour, that he has been in flea markets and he has never been employed. He does not remember the catering school that he went to. He doesn't remember whether that was ten years ago or five years ago. He has absolutely no clue. He's a waiter, he says, and he went to catering school to become a waiter. Your Honour, there is simply not enough information and evidence produced before this Court before -- with which you can make a judicial assessment. In national jurisdictions, courts will inquire into the criminal record of an accused, is there a social workers' report, his ties to the Bijeljina community, his ties -- continued ties with the Prijedor region, what connections he still has with the people in Prijedor, there is no information available to this Trial Chamber on any of this matters. His economic status, while in -- and counsel's motion he says his family has had regular income since his surrender in 2002. From where does this income, come from? What other ties does he have? He goes on to assert that he will not interfere with witnesses and victims. He also says that he learned of the indictment in April 2002, and he had a chance to intimidate or harm the victims or potential witness and that he still not do so. Perhaps he did not do so, Your Honour, because he didn't know who they were. Now, Your Honours, he has, with full disclosure made by the Prosecution, got sufficient names and information as to who these witnesses are and where they are. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution respectfully submits that this Court is unable to make a proper evaluation. We still, despite the fact that the accused has come to this Court and given his testimony here, we still are in the dark as to what he's been doing and his future conduct must be predicated on his past. The crimes committed by the accused, Your Honour, are crimes of exceptional violence and human depravity. Your Honours it's important to note that the accused was not in a position of authority or in the military or any police hierarchy. He was not a man who can claim he was swept along with the tide and became morally anaesthetised and performed certain official tasks to excess. This man, Your Honours, went to the camps with the sole and particular purpose of beating and killing civilians who had already been incarcerated by violence and force. He took a sadistic and perverse pleasure and the repeated and premeditated nature of the abuses are all additional factors which no doubt will be considered to be aggravating factors if convicted by this Court. Zoran Zigic, Your Honour, who he committed similar crimes with, was in fact convicted and sentenced to 25 years, although this particular judgement is under appeal. There is nothing before this Chamber that ought to convince any court in a national or indeed an international jurisdiction that a man capable of such moral depravity to the point of amorality can be considered safe for this Court to provisionally release. Your Honour, the fact that he says he did not know he was a wanted man, there has been no credible explanation forthcoming from the accused, so we cannot presume it is genuine. That indeed that was the case. It is stretching the credulity of this Court to ask you to believe that living in Prijedor as he did, with this -- the Omarska case on television, with his name being mentioned, that no -- absolutely no one mentioned to him that his friend, Zoran Zigic is at The Hague facing the charges before him. There is nothing to say that he had no knowledge whatsoever that he knew that he was wanted by this Tribunal. It is an opportunistic argument at best, Your Honour, seeing that this was -- he was publicly indicted and there were -- was also the indictment was also published in the bulletins of the Tribunal. Your Honour, it is our -- Prosecution's respectful submission that there is nothing before this honour upon which this court can make a judicial evaluation, and if it does so, it will be an error in law. Unless there is something else I could assist Your Honours on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, short reply. First, it's time for a little truth. I made out a typo, I left out the word no source of income. I apologise to the Prosecution. I apologise to the Court. Couple of other things rather quickly, she says no national jurisdiction would allow pre-trial release for persons charged with serious offences looking at serious sentences. That's not a direct quote. Those are my words. The jurisdiction with which I'm most familiar provides --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please so down for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Provides a right to bond in all cases with, like I think there are two exceptions. One exception is a case where the Prosecution is seeking the death penalty and provides evidence to the Court that, one, the defendant did it and, two, there is proof evident that he will get the death penalty. That's jurisdiction I'm the most familiar with. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does it work in practice, never mind the right? How does it work in practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour my firm has had more than one client who has been charged with -- or lawyers who office in my firm's offices, because it was a lawyer that leased space from us and had clients who were charged with the death -- with capital murder where the Prosecution was seeking the death penalty, they were granted bond, they made bond, and they showed up in court. And I might add that the one I'm thinking of was acquitted. But setting that aside, line 23 or page 23, line 24, of the transcript, the Prosecutor said that Mr. Knezevic was charged with 31 counts of murder and then later I believe Judge Robinson she referred you to schedules E and F; is that correct? You asked the question, E and F, of the indictment? I just went through E and F rather quickly and I may be a little off but I counted five murders, not 31, on those two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. schedules. I counted other charges but only five murders and I may be one or two off. I did it quickly and they are sometimes hard to read. Judge, the Prosecution has presented an indictment. An indictment is a charge. Just because a person is indicted for an offence doesn't mean as the Prosecutor would have one believe that he is guilty, that he is a depraved person, that he has committed these crimes, when the Prosecution has presented nothing but its pleadings to this Trial Chamber as to Mr. Knezevic's guilt. We have met the burden, we have done everything we can to show you that we can -- that there are conditions of release which would guarantee both his appearance in court and we presented a plan to you that would do as much as possible to guarantee the safety of the public, victims and witnesses. Your Honour, we can't do any more. The Prosecution would have -- would make provisional release an impossible burden. They would make it a dream that no one could ever have. No matter what a defendant does, the Prosecutor would raise the bar. One could never jump over the bar they keep setting -- they keep raising. Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall give the Prosecution two weeks to respond, if at all, to investigate and respond to the matters of which they had no notice today. We will then render our judgement. This matter is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.12 p.m. 25
